doc.title: Joe Segal — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Goofing off in the Army and no famous musicians
summary: He explains his failed radio training, a one-performance try at an entertainment MOS, and that Billy Byers was the most famous musician he met.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: What was your - in the service - what was your... what did they have you do?
Your MOS, thank you very much.

What do they call it when you goof off? I forget the term, anyhow. I spent one year, eleven months, and what was it, twelve days or something trying to get out as soon as I got in. Gold brick or something. I was supposed to learn radio and aircraft radio repair, and I was foolish enough to fluff it off because I wasn’t interested. I probably could’ve been into electronics pretty heavily today. But I wasn’t. I even tried changing my MOS from Clerk Typist to Entertainment. I played drums and sang, and it must have
been terrible, because I lasted for one performance and they changed it back again. Yeah, it’s fun. But the best part was coming into Chicago.

Did you see any of the - I mean there was a lot of jazz musicians that of course were drafted in the service. Did you run across any of those musicians of that time? I know Joe, once again Joe Wilder’s one of those individuals that come to mind, because the Philly connection, but of course he ended up enrolling or volunteering for the Marines. But there are a lot of... Hal McIntyre, a lot of musicians...
I didn’t meet any famous ones.
I guess the most famous one was Billy Byers.
